lines.text: Riya searches her college notice board for placement drive. Zero results. But the notice is right there: campus recruitment starts Monday.
Keyword search matches letters, and these two phrases share no words. She needs a search that matches meaning.
An embedding model does exactly that. Give it any text, and it returns a fixed-length list of numbers: for example, fifteen hundred and thirty-six of them.
No single number means anything alone. Together, they work like coordinates: one point in a very large space.
Here is that space, flattened to two dimensions. Placement drive lands right beside campus recruitment.
Biryani recipe lands far away. The model was trained on huge numbers of text pairs, so close points mean similar things.
Now Riya's search is simple: embed the query, and return the nearest points.
The same idea powers RAG, and matching your resume to a job description.
Two rules. First, embed documents and queries with the same model. Every model draws its own map.
Second, similar is not the same as true. I love DSA and I hate DSA often land close together.
So here's the line to remember: an embedding turns meaning into a position. Close together means similar meaning.
Next lesson: cosine similarity from scratch with NumPy.
